item.title: Topology Construction Algorithms for DECT NR+ in Normal and Ultra-Dense Deployments
item.description: arXiv:2610.12671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The 5G-grade DECT NR+ technology designed to support massive machine-type communications (mMTC) relies on the decentralized mesh connectivity concept. The currently utilized topology construction algorithms are very sensitive to the node density, which causes interference at the node association phase and may lead to instable topologies. In this study, we propose several algorithms that need to be utilized at relay and leaf nodes to allow stabilization of the topology: (i) load-dependent relay allocation, (ii) hysteresis-based association control, (iii) blacklist-based association control, and (iv) smart beacon placement. Due to the complex interference structure in DECT NR+ mesh systems, we utilize system-level simulations to assess the performance in both normal and ultra-dense conditions in terms of the efficiency of topology construction and the performance characteristics of the resulting topology. Our results show that dense DECT NR+ networks do suffer from topology instability, with reassociation rates exceeding 10 per second and recovery times lasting over 10 minutes. By implementing the proposed mechanisms, the network dynamically scales, reducing the number of required relays by more than half, from 34% to 15%. They also stabilize the topology by reducing the reassociation rates to just 2-3 per second allowing large-scale networks of several hundred nodes to operate efficiently.
item.dc:creator: Andrey Samuylov, Dmitri Moltchanov, Roman Glazkov, Juho Pirskanen, Jussi Numminen, Mikko Valkama

item.title: PCM: Programmable Congestion Management for Terabit RDMA NICs
item.description: arXiv:2610.13130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Datacenter congestion control (CC) and load balancing (LB) evolve rapidly as workload demands change, but deployment depends on RDMA hardware and transport interfaces. Emerging programmable RDMA engines tie policy code to vendor APIs. Operators must therefore port each policy for every platform they deploy. We address this with PCM, a programming model that separates portable congestion management from platform integration on datacenter NICs. Developers write event-driven handlers that they can debug in simulation and reuse on real hardware. PCM exposes flow telemetry as signals and uses triggers to support per-event reactions and coarser responses to accumulated feedback. Vendors provide optimized backends that map signals and output controls to native NIC mechanisms with defined feedback and control semantics. We demonstrate PCM's expressivity by implementing eleven well-known datacenter CC and LB algorithms. We deploy PCM across four distinct datapaths: an Ultra Ethernet simulator, CPU-based UCCL, and on-NIC offloads on NVIDIA ConnectX-8 and Microsoft 1P. On CX-8, PCM-Swift achieves processing capacity equivalent to one reaction per three 4 KiB packets at 800 Gbit/s, using one-fifth of the NIC's hardware threads. In UCCL, it matches native Swift's 1.56 Tbit/s goodput with 64 KiB chunk-level control. PCM's design informed ongoing Ultra Ethernet work toward a portable congestion management interface.
item.dc:creator: Mikhail Khalilov, Timo Schneider, Tommaso Bonato, Siyuan Shen, Marcin Chrapek, Yehor Kozyr, Alberto Merino, Rip Sohan, Surendra Anubolu, Mohan Kalkunte, Ahmad Ghalayini, Abdul Kabbani, Torsten Hoefler

item.title: Configuration Migration Planning through Decoupled Modeling and Searching
item.description: arXiv:2610.13161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Executing large network configuration changes, called migrations, is slow and error-prone today; operators must manually devise a safe order for updating devices that does not disrupt traffic and meets operational intents (e.g., low total time). We develop Smoothie, a versatile migration planning framework that, unlike existing tools, can support diverse operational intents. Inspired by automated planning, it achieves versatility by decoupling the encoding of network safety and intents from the search for a viable plan. Smoothie uses symbolic simulation for general and scalable safety encoding, after which it can use a range of planners, including existing off-the-shelf planners and a new one we developed for optimized parallel plans. We demonstrate Smoothie's versatility and benchmark its performance using diverse migration scenarios on many topologies. It finds both sequential plans and parallel plans, and the parallel ones compress up to thousands of configuration updates into no more than 3 steps. Its versatility does not come at the expense of performance: finishing most planning tasks in less than 1 hour.
item.dc:creator: Dan Wang, Peng Zhang, Ratul Mahajan

item.title: Maneuver Coordination Using V2I to Improve Traffic Efficiency at Intersections
item.description: arXiv:2610.13394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traffic efficiency and air pollutants are major issues in urban transport systems, as they are critical points for traffic flows and people living in urban areas, respectively. In response to this challenge, connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) have garnered increasing attention, with the potential to address the above challenges through cooperative maneuvering and real-time communication. In this paper, we consider an intersection served by a multi-access edge computing (MEC) where CAVs communicate with a controller to pass the intersection without the need of signals and without stopping unless in presence of heavy congestion. For this purpose, we propose a first-in-first-scheduled (FIFS) algorithm, and we specify the communication protocol for its practical implementation. The solution is validated through simulations with varying traffic densities, showing that it provides significant gains in travel time and emissions compared to both uncontrolled intersections, with or without traffic lights, and a benchmark solution derived from the literature.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Farina, Marco Rapelli, Barbara Mav\`i Masini, Claudio Casetti, Alessandro Bazzi

item.title: On the Alignment Between Spectral Efficiency and Positioning Accuracy in Multi-LEO Clusters
item.description: arXiv:2610.13526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are expected to play a key role in future 6G Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTNs), where dense deployments enable cooperative multi-satellite processing for communication and positioning. While existing works have addressed communication and localization objectives separately, the correlation and alignment between these objectives remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the correlation between Spectral Efficiency (SE) and positioning accuracy in cooperative multi-LEO satellite clusters. We consider an uplink direct-to-device scenario in which multiple satellites jointly process user signals and evaluate cluster performance using SE and Position Error Bound (PEB) metrics. We derive Time-of-Arrival (TOA)-based and Doppler-based PEBs, while communication performance is quantified through the achievable SE under joint signal processing. Using realistic LEO constellation simulations, we demonstrate that for clusters of seven satellites, SE exhibits a strong negative correlation with Doppler-based PEB (correlation coefficient of $-0.72$). In contrast, its correlation with TOA-based PEB is notably weaker, ranging between $-0.55$ and $-0.37$. These findings suggest that communication-oriented LEO clusters are largely compatible with Doppler-based positioning, but not necessarily with TOA-based positioning.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Kapoglis, Sharief Saleh, Henk Wymeersch, Hazem Sallouha

item.title: RAPID: Proactive Rate Control for Enabling High Data Rate and Low Latency in 5G Edge Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.13749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many 6G use cases such as tactile Internet and eXtended reality applications would simultaneously require a high data rate and low latency wireless connectivity.It is increasingly being realized that the current transport protocols relying on packet loss and delay are insufficient to satisfy the data rate and latency requirements of such applications. To address this problem, we propose RAPID, a transport layer solution designed for private 5G edge networks, where the bottleneck is located at the base station. We show that by regulating the send rate to maintain a target physical resource block utilization, we can achieve high data rate, low latency communication. We design a simple yet effective policy that adapts to the dynamic nature of wireless channel conditions. In a multi-UE scenario with two RAPID flows and one TCP Cubic flow, our testbed results show that RAPID flows achieve significant improvements in one-way delay, i.e., 72x and 55x lower compared to TCP Cubic, with negligible packet loss at the cost of modest goodput reductions of 16% and 27%, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Hamid Hassani, Sonia M. Heemstra de Groot, Ignas G. Niemegeers, Kishor C. Joshi, George Exarchakos

item.title: One-Way Delay Model for 5G Low Latency, High Data Rate Communications
item.description: arXiv:2610.13761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Achieving low delay and high data rate communication in 5G requires preventing persistent queue backlogs at path bottlenecks. A key indicator of queue buildup is an increase in one-way delay (OWD) of packets. However, accurately measuring OWD is challenging due to synchronization issues between the sender and receiver. Moreover, using OWD to infer the onset of queueing can be inefficient. For instance, congestion control mechanisms that rely on latency as a congestion signal may result in cellular network underutilization, see, e.g., [1]. Thus, to develop more efficient rate control approaches, it is crucial not only to estimate OWD accurately but also to perform a more fine-grained analysis that provides detailed insights into the queue status. This paper presents a framework for modeling OWD in 5G edge networks, where the wireless link is typically the path bottleneck. %, by modeling it through measurable delay components. We demonstrate that OWD is dominated by queueing delay (QD), particularly at high data rates. We analyze QD by decomposing it into two main components: aggregation delay and channel access time. Aggregation delay can be accurately measured at the user equipment (UE), and channel access time can be estimated based on network conditions. Our key contribution shows that QD, while challenging to measure directly at the base station (BS), can be closely approximated by combining these components. We validate this model through NS3 simulations under varying network loads and single- and multi-UE scenarios. This framework provides a foundation for developing advanced mechanisms for congestion control and bottleneck detection in 5G networks.
item.dc:creator: Hamid Hassani, Sonia M. Heemstra de Groot, Ignas G. Niemegeers, Kishor C. Joshi, George Exarchakos

item.title: Goal-Oriented Bundle Management and Flow Control for Deep-Space Communications via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.13923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep-space communications operate under intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and relay storage constraints. In such networks, the Bundle Protocol enables store-carry-forward communication, requiring relay nodes to manage limited storage and scarce contact opportunities. Relay-side scheduling and dropping decisions are inherently goal-oriented: transmission resources should be allocated to bundles most valuable to downstream mission objectives. Conventional schedulers, such as FIFO, do not explicitly optimize task utility and may provide unfair service across heterogeneous planetary sources. This paper presents a closed-loop modeling and learning framework for relay-side bundle and flow management in a contact-driven deep-space network, where lunar and Martian updates are forwarded through a shared-buffer relay to Earth. We quantify destination-side information freshness using excess age $\Delta_i^e(t)=[\Delta_i(t)-d_i(t)]^+$, where $\Delta_i(t)$ denotes the Age of Information of source $i$ and $d_i(t)$ is a source-dependent delay baseline. Based on this metric, we define a goal-oriented loss that supports source-dependent nonlinear penalties, allowing prioritization according to mission relevance. We formulate relay control as a constrained semi-Markov decision process (CSMDP) and solve it using masked Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Feasibility-aware action masking restricts transmissions to bundles that can complete within the remaining contact window. DTNSim simulations indicate improved age-based utility and inter-flow fairness compared with baseline schedulers. The proposed framework jointly optimizes relay-side bundle scheduling, dropping, and flow control under contact-driven dynamics with explicit fairness considerations across heterogeneous sources.
item.dc:creator: Sajjad Baghaeea, Aimin Lib, Shanmugarajan Balasubramanian, Elif Uysal

item.title: Deploying RDMA for Large-Scale Inference and Training Workloads
item.description: arXiv:2610.12815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: RDMA can reduce communication overhead in distributed machine learning systems, but realizing these benefits in production requires more than replacing TCP. Variable-size messages, concurrent connections, bursty incasts, and service failures introduce challenges that hardware offload alone cannot address. This paper reports our experience deploying ByteExpress, a software communication layer over hardware RDMA, in ByteDance's parameter-server-based inference and training systems. We present three lessons from the deployment: efficient RDMA requires buffer management across application and transport layers; scalable communication requires coordinated management of connections, receive capacity, and outstanding data; and service availability requires recovery above the transport layer. ByteExpress combines an RDMA-aware allocator, zero-copy transfers, QP multiplexing, receive-credit flow control, a software send window, and RPC-assisted recovery. In production inference, ByteExpress reduces mean and P99 model parameter fetch latency by 35.7% and 43.7%, respectively, and total CPU usage by 10.69% compared with kernel TCP. In training, ByteExpress reduces P99 model parameter push latency by up to 74.0% compared with TCP, with no PFC pauses observed at runtime.
item.dc:creator: Yibo Huang, Yi Cui, Yukai Huang, Huaping Zhou, Jiancong Tong, Zhaoyu Wu, Gen Miao, Haoran Wei, Boyan Ding, Zhuo Jiang, Jianxi Ye, Yibo Zhu, Chuanxiong Guo, Yang Xu, Jie Wu

item.title: Post-Quantum Session Establishment for Matter over Thread: Message Size, Transport, and Protocol Options
item.description: arXiv:2610.13026v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. We quantify the cost of moving CASE to ML-KEM and post-quantum signatures over Thread, where frames carry at most 127 bytes and a Matter message at most 1178 bytes. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. As a first step, hybrid P-256+ML-KEM-512 key exchange with a cached device chain protects session keys against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks while every message still fits the current limit.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Commey

item.title: Agentic Peer-to-Peer Networks: From Content Distribution to Capability and Action Sharing
item.description: arXiv:2603.03753v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The ongoing shift of Artificial Intelligence (AI) from centralized cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) to local inference on edge devices is enabling Client-Side Autonomous Agents (CSAAs) - persistent personal agents that can plan, access local context, and invoke tools on behalf of users. As these agents collaborate directly, they form Agentic Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Networks. Unlike classic overlays exchanging static, hash-indexed content (e.g., BitTorrent), agentic P2P exchanges dynamic, heterogeneous capabilities that are potentially unsafe, requiring semantic discovery, drift management, and risk-aware execution. We outline the networking foundations for such collaboration. To organize this design space, we propose a plane-based reference architecture decoupling connectivity, semantic discovery, and execution. To support discovery under drift, we introduce signed, soft-state capability descriptors to support intent-aware routing. Finally, to cope with adversarial settings, we present a tiered verification spectrum - ranging from reputation signals (Tier 1) and canary probes (Tier 2) to cryptographic evidence (Tier 3) - that aligns trust costs with task risks. Results from a proxy-level discrete-event simulation suggest improved workflow success under poisoning and drift with modest control-plane overhead.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: T. Wang, L. You, J. Tong, C. Zhao, and S. Zhang, "Agentic Peer-to-Peer Networks: From Content Distribution to Capability and Action Sharing," IEEE Communications Magazine, Early Access, pp. 1-7, Oct. 2026
item.dc:creator: Taotao Wang, Lizhao You, Jingwen Tong, Chonghe Zhao, Shengli Zhang

item.title: Fairness-Guided DQN-Based TXOP Control for NR-U/Wi-Fi Coexistence
item.description: arXiv:2605.00457v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: New Radio operating in unlicensed spectrum (NR-U) and Wi-Fi employ different contention parameters and channel-occupancy durations, which can produce severe coexistence imbalance. This correspondence develops a fairness-guided deep Q-network (DQN) that adjusts the NR-U transmission opportunity (TXOP) using the observed per-node throughput ratio. Two reward designs, Q1 and Q2, expose complementary operating regimes. Q1 promotes strict per-node throughput balance, whereas Q2 admits a broader inter-radio-access-technology fairness region and rewards throughput improvement in an intermediate fairness band. The policies are compared with the default Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) listen-before-talk (LBT), an adapted multi-armed-bandit method, a utility-fairness-based tabular Q-learning comparator, and a default-referenced fixed-TXOP baseline. Experiments across four priority classes and asymmetric populations report aggregate throughput, user-level Jain fairness, and concave throughput utility over 20 independent trials. The results characterize the cost of strict fairness, efficiency recovery under moderate relaxation, and transfer from symmetric to asymmetric deployments.
item.dc:creator: Po-Heng Chou, Yi-Fang Yu, Shou-Yu Chen, Chiapin Wang

item.title: Mode 0: Architecture, Risk Taxonomy, and Standardization Pathway for RCU-Assisted V2X Safety Communication
item.description: arXiv:2605.25431v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The 3GPP V2X resource allocation framework offers two entity classes for coordinating vehicle communication --- base-station scheduling and autonomous vehicle selection --- a design space we show to be structurally incomplete for safety-critical coordination. We propose Mode 0, a third entity class centered on the Roadside Computing Unit (RCU): infrastructure integrating elevated sensing, sidelink communication, and local computation, owned by traffic management authorities rather than network operators. We formalize Mode 0's subfamily taxonomy (Mode 0a through 0c), its traffic risk taxonomy and mandatory-escalation boundary, its cross-domain coexistence with Modes 1--4, and its standardization pathway. Of the three failure modes motivating this proposal --- scheduling saturation, occlusion-driven information gaps, and an institutional authority gap during severe hazards --- only scheduling is evaluated by simulation; information and authority are argued architecturally and evidenced by independent deployment convergence across Chinese local and industry-alliance standards, Chinese operator infrastructure, and European and US C-V2X programs, properties no channel-level simulation can instantiate. In a multi-agent reinforcement learning simulation (88 training runs, 95% confidence intervals), per-vehicle policies (Mode 0c) raise worst-interval delivery reliability at the critical safety load from 0.217 under shared per-class policies (Mode 0a) to 0.792, cutting lost safety messages from 38% to 6%. An idealized model of standardized sensing-based semi-persistent scheduling loses 10% at the same load, and per-vehicle coordination more than halves the longest gaps between safety updates against it (3.9 against 8.4 message periods). With spare spectrum, a safety partition sized by the RCU delivers every safety message. We call for a 3GPP study item to formalize Mode 0.
item.dc:creator: Dewei Jiang (Nantong University), Xiang Gu (Nantong University)

item.title: Extended Version: Measuring the End-to-End Resilience of Application Deployments in Real-World Communication Networks with DRACO
item.description: arXiv:2608.10611v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Billions of users take Internet connectivity for granted and use it daily to access applications deployed anywhere around the globe. What users perceive as a seamless connection between their end device and the application server involves a complex system of systems operated by various actors. Failures in any of these systems disrupt user-to-application connectivity if the communication network is not resilient. Since communication networks are a critical infrastructure as part of ICT, real-world operators rarely disclose information about them. This makes it difficult to measure the end-to-end resilience of deployments, because it requires guessing topologies and the availability of the involved systems. This paper presents DRACO, a framework for modeling communication networks and measuring end-to-end resilience of application deployments. It enables configuring application deployments across arbitrary communication networks and evaluating their availability, robustness, and resilience. We demonstrate the functional scope of DRACO by modeling nationwide application deployments in Germany and France, highlighting its compatibility with a wide variety of public data sources and synthetic data.
item.dc:creator: Leon Janzen, Matthias Hollick

item.title: Energy-Aware Receiver-initiated MAC Protocol for Energy Harvesting IoT
item.description: arXiv:2610.11492v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Energy harvesting (EH) technology has emerged as a key approach for extending the operational autonomy of Internet of Things (IoT) devices. In this context, medium access control (MAC) protocols for EH-IoT make use of the harvested energy efficiently to enhance the application performance. However, many existing MAC protocols rely on stored energy the battery in devising energy-aware strategies, which can interrupt the device operation and hinder the execution of ongoing tasks in dynamic and low EH conditions. To address this, this paper presents an energy-aware receiver-initiated MAC protocol for EH-IoT devices, called EARI-MAC, that adjusts the duty cycle of the receiver device based on stored energy and current harvesting power using the mathematical formulation. This approach supports sustained receiver operation under low EH conditions and improved application performance when harvested energy is abundant. The performance of the EARI-MAC has been evaluated in simulation using the real solar data gathered in Novi Sad, for three consecutive days. The simulation results demonstrate that the EARI-MAC utilizes the available energy resources efficiently and improves the packet delivery ratio and network throughput by more than 10%, reduces the receiver energy consumption by 5.6% and 8.2% and energy consumption per bit by 9.6% and 13.9% compared with QPPD-MAC and energy-unaware MAC, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Sohail Sarang, Praveen Kumar Donta, Dejan Vukobratovi\'c

item.title: Optimizing Entanglement Distribution Protocols: Maximizing Classical Information in Quantum Networks
item.description: arXiv:2603.25360v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large-scale quantum networks depend on the efficient distribution of entangled pairs between distant nodes. However, state-of-the-art solutions rely on restrictive operational assumptions, incur prohibitive computational complexity, and optimize metrics misaligned with application needs. This paper addresses the entanglement distribution problem introducing four pivotal advances. First, since the primary application of quantum communication is private information transmission, we derive the Ensemble Capacity, a novel metric that quantifies the private classical information enabled by entanglement distribution. Second, we propose a generalized formulation of the Entanglement Distribution Problem that allows arbitrary sequencing of entanglement swapping and purification, removing the structural restrictions of prior models. Third, to navigate the resulting combinatorial space, we introduce a dynamic programming-based hypergraph generation algorithm that preserves exact, continuous fidelities, avoiding quantization, while pruning sub-optimal sequences in advance. Finally, we integrate these solutions into CODE, a two-tier orchestration framework enabling near-real-time network operation. Extensive evaluations show that our approach achieves higher private information capacity and significantly lower computational complexity than existing solutions, while meeting the sub-second latency requirements of dynamic quantum network operation.
item.dc:creator: Ethan Sanchez Hidalgo, Diego Zafra Bono, Guillermo Encinas Lago, J. Xavier Salvat Lozano, Jose A. Ayala-Romero, Xavier Costa Perez

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Intent Fulfilment and Assurance for 6G RAN
item.description: arXiv:2607.08809v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Intent-based network management automates 6G service lifecycles, but existing fulfilment and assurance approaches require traffic inspection, per-flow tracking, or vendor-internal telemetry. These requirements conflict with privacy constraints in multi-tenant networks and vendor opacity in O-RAN deployments. We present an architecture that provisions resources from declared intent categories without traffic inspection and verifies fulfilment using only cell-level standardised PM counters at the O1 interface. A data-processing inequality bounds resource-allocation leakage about traffic content by $\log_2 K$ bits for $K$ categories. Intent-traffic unlinkability and node-opaque verification hold by construction. If verification requires at least $q$ cells per category among $M$ cells, the ceiling becomes $\log_2 \lfloor M/q \rfloor$ bits. This bound covers the category/resource channel, not total inference from PM counters. When individual records add state-independent noise to the category aggregate, the category-mean verifier is at least as powerful as any per-agent verifier. We map the architecture to the 3GPP intent lifecycle and O-RAN Non-RT RIC. On production PM data from four operator networks, the category-mean score has higher AUC on three networks and comparable AUC on the fourth under category-wide replacement, while per-cell screening suits sparse faults. These injection-based experiments do not establish the theorem's observation premise. Within-period cell co-movement limits a category mean to the evidence of 6 to 14 independent cells, and category-level verifiers need per-category calibration.
item.dc:creator: Joss Armstrong
